source.title: Scaling Laws and Spectra of Shallow Neural Networks in the Feature Learning Regime
source.authors: Leonardo Defilippis; Yi-Zhou Xu; Julius Girardin; Emanuele Troiani; Vittorio Erba; Lenka Zdeborová; Bruno Loureiro; Florent Krzakala

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some mathematical notation is flattened or imperfectly rendered, but the study is identifiable and its main results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper derives piecewise scaling regimes, plateaus, and crossovers in shallow-network excess risk, qualifying the idea that a single power law describes scaling curves. It does not test language-model pretraining laws directly.
record.gate_note: The study analyzes excess risk for diagonal and quadratic shallow networks as a function of effective sample size and weight decay. It does not report held-out language-model pretraining loss or sweeps over language-model parameters, tokens, or compute. Its own excess-risk results bear on V7's curve-bending component. Weight-spectrum results and comparisons between state-evolution predictions and simulations are not additional measurements of the claim's language-model outcomes.
record.test_reason: This is a theory paper on synthetic teacher-student regression with shallow diagonal and quadratic networks. It derives how excess risk scales with sample size and weight decay, then checks the rates with small simulations (d of 100 to 800). It never trains or measures a language model, and it does not vary parameters, tokens or compute. So no row measures what V1–V7 name, by the same kind of system. Even V7, which concerns fit-dependence and bending of published LM scaling laws, is not measured. The authors say only that their plateaus and crossovers mirror the empirical LM literature. I record the findings under fits_no_version instead of treating them as a T5 test of V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but incomplete. The authors derive a phase diagram of excess-risk scaling laws, with plateaus and crossovers, that is universal across diagonal and quadratic networks. A second main conclusion is missing from the record: the spectral features of the trained weights map onto underfitting, overfitting and approximation error. They present this as a first-principles basis for heavy-tail spectrum–generalization observations. The state-evolution extension beyond proportional asymptotics is heuristic, supported numerically, and left as a conjecture.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies supervised ERM for shallow diagonal and quadratic networks using LASSO/matrix-compressed-sensing mappings and approximate-message-passing state evolution. It does not use autoregressive language-model pretraining or the original language-model scaling-law measurement setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported excess-risk rate changes with effective sample size and regularization strength; diagonal and quadratic networks also differ in the Phase V function ρ.

fits_no_version.finding: In noisy teacher-student ERM with diagonal and quadratic shallow networks, excess risk vs effective sample size follows a phase diagram with several features. It shows plateaus, distinct power-law rates, crossovers set by weight decay, harmful overfitting, and a λ^(-2/3) interpolation peak. Simulations (d = 100–800) agree with the predicted rates (Fig. 3, Fig. 8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In shallow feature-learning networks, sample-scaling of excess risk is piecewise power-law, with regime-dependent exponents set by sample size and regularization.

fits_no_version.finding: With weight decay tuned optimally, the excess risk reaches Bayes-optimal rates. These are n_eff^(-1+1/(2γ)) below d^(2γ) and d/n_eff above it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal regularization removes the harmful-overfitting phase and attains Bayes-optimal sample-scaling rates in these shallow networks.

fits_no_version.finding: Without label noise, the phase diagram is simpler and shared by both architectures. The rate is n_eff^(1-2γ) for n_eff ≪ d (Result 4, Fig. 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Noiseless sample-scaling rates in shallow feature-learning networks are faster and universal across architectures.

record.problems: The main rates are asymptotic/theoretical characterizations, and the extension of state evolution beyond its rigorously proven proportional-asymptotic regime is heuristic. The authors state that non-asymptotic multiplicative bounds remain an open problem. The study's outcomes are shallow-network excess risk, not language-model pretraining loss.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant result rows omitted. Weight-spectrum results and supplementary spectrum simulations were not included because they do not measure the scaling outcomes named by the claim.

untested.parts: No LM held-out loss vs parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No depth/width comparison at fixed parameter count.
No practical models in other modalities or regimes; only synthetic teacher-student regression.
No comparison of published LM law fits, parameter counting, schedules or fitting methods; no LM loss curves.

missing.what: Noiseless (Δ=0) excess-risk rates and their phase diagram
Simulation-vs-theory agreement on decay rates across phases, d = 100–800, three λ values
Ridge (L2) linear baseline gives trivial risk for n ≪ d, i.e. is suboptimal

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V7 link was dropped. V7 concerns disagreement among published LM scaling-law fits and bending of LM loss curves. This paper only analyses synthetic shallow-network regression, scaled in samples and weight decay rather than parameters or compute. Its link to LM laws is by analogy, which the authors themselves call mirroring. If curators judge that theoretical toy-model scaling results should count toward V5 or V7, the rows would read as observed piecewise power laws under limits_scope. The text gives no LM-level evidence either way.

versions.untested_parts: No language-model held-out pretraining loss or scaling sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No fitting on small runs followed by prediction of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between model parameters and training tokens; optimal weight decay is not that allocation.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study considers shallow feature-learning networks, but does not test whether language-model pretraining laws carry over to other modalities or training regimes.
No downstream-task performance or relation between downstream performance and pretraining loss.

The paper shows phase-dependent excess-risk rates and crossovers in shallow networks, but does not compare language-model scaling-law fits, compute-optimal parameter/token exponents, or fitting choices such as parameter counting and training schedule.
